title: List of Forms and Contact Details Required to Request Medical Records From Johns Hopkins Medicine in 2026

Requesting medical records from Johns Hopkins Medicine means identifying the right facility, picking the right authorization form, and sending it to the right Health Information Management office. With nine submission destinations across Maryland, Washington D.C., and Florida, each with its own contacts and procedures, sending to the wrong one delays processing. For personal injury firms, that gets worse when a client was treated at several Hopkins locations.[Codes Health](https://www.getcodeshealth.com/) handles facility identification, form validation, and persistent follow-up through one platform, working toward complete records in a couple of weeks rather than months.


## **Key Takeaways**


-


Johns Hopkins Medicine lists nine medical-record submission destinations, each with its own authorization requirements and contact details


-


Johns Hopkins says applicable law generally allows[21 to 30 days](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/patient-care/patients-visitors/medical-records) depending on the state, though requests often finish sooner


-


Johns Hopkins says a $6.50 fee may apply to electronically maintained records, while paper or microfilm portions may be charged up to[$0.12 per page](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/patient-care/patients-visitors/medical-records) plus a $0.90 flat labor fee, with costs varying by facility


-


Submission methods vary by location. Suburban Hospital states that attorney and insurance-company requests must be mailed or delivered in person


-


MyChart gives immediate access to some finalized results and notes, but may not contain the entire record, so litigation work still needs formal HIM requests


-


Incomplete authorizations are a leading cause of denied requests, and pre-submission validation can prevent the corrected resubmissions that add time to a case


## **Understanding Johns Hopkins Medical Records**


### **Your Right to Access Your Records**


Under HIPAA, a covered entity generally must act on an individual's access request within 30 calendar days, with one possible extension of up to 30 additional days if the individual gets timely written notice. Johns Hopkins says applicable law generally allows between 21 and 30 days depending on the state, and that requests typically do not take that long. Maryland law separately addresses disclosure within a reasonable time, with a 21-working-day provision tied to knowing refusal. Because Hopkins operates in Maryland, D.C., and Florida, the governing rule depends on where the records sit.


For attorneys and other third parties, access requires a patient-signed authorization matching the request type and facility.


### **What the Record Contains**


A complete Johns Hopkins record may include:


-


**Clinical documentation:** history and physicals, progress notes, consultation reports, and discharge summaries


-


**Diagnostic results:** laboratory values, pathology reports, and radiology interpretations


-


**Treatment records:** operative notes, anesthesia records, medication administration records, and nursing flow sheets


-


**Administrative documents:** consent forms, billing statements, and insurance correspondence


Nursing notes and MAR documentation can carry timeline detail that matters in litigation, and Johns Hopkins states that MyChart may not contain a patient's entire medical record.


## **Initiating a Records Request**


### **Online Options**


Patients can use the MyChart portal at mychart.hopkinsmedicine.org. Test results and provider clinic notes can be viewed as soon as they are finalized. When a patient requests a downloadable copy of broader health records through the Sharing Hub, Johns Hopkins says processing could take several business days depending on the size and type of the request. Large-volume requests may not be available through MyChart at all, in which case Hopkins directs users to HIM.


### **Mail and Fax Submission**


For formal requests:


1.


**Identify the correct facility** using billing statements, appointment paperwork, or MyChart account information


2.


**Download the right form** from the[official records page](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/patient-care/patients-visitors/medical-records)


3.


**Complete all required fields** , including demographics, date ranges, record types, and delivery method


4.


**Sign and date the form**


5.


**Follow the submission instructions for that specific location** , since methods vary. Suburban Hospital states that attorney and insurance-company requests must be mailed or delivered in person with the signed patient release


Keeping fax confirmations and using certified mail are reasonable firm practices, though Hopkins does not publish a required follow-up interval.


For firms running multiple Hopkins matters at once,[Codes Health](https://www.getcodeshealth.com/) removes the manual coordination by handling facility identification, submission, and follow-up across locations from one place.


## **Johns Hopkins Authorization Forms**


Johns Hopkins provides several request and authorization forms for different requester and provider types, plus a separate form for requesting amendments to protected health information.


**Request by Patient or Patient Representative, Form A.6.2.a.1**


-


Patient requesting their own records


**Authorization for Release, Hospitals, Form A.2.1.c**


-


Third-party requests for hospital records


**Authorization for Release, Mental Health, Form A.2.1.l**


-


Psychiatric and psychological records


**Authorization for Release, JHCP, Form A.2.1.dG**


-


Community Physicians outpatient records


**Authorization for Release, Home Care, Form A.2.1.bH**


-


Home health and hospice records


**Authorization for Release, All Other, Form A.2.1.a**


-


Other Johns Hopkins providers


**Request to Amend PHI, Form A.6.3.a**


-


Corrections to medical records, not a release authorization


### **Completing the Form Correctly**


Every authorization needs the patient's full legal name, date of birth, and current address; the dates of service; explicit authorization for each record type; the delivery method; and the patient or authorized representative's signature with date.


On expiration, HIPAA requires an authorization to contain an expiration date or event, but that does not always mean writing a date into a blank. The current Hopkins hospital form provides that if the expiration blank is left empty, the authorization expires one year after signing.


On dates, give a clear range whenever you can. Hopkins forms request dates of service and state that, unless otherwise specified, records will generally be provided for the past five years.


### **Common Pitfalls**


-


Missing signatures, which stop a request before it starts


-


Wrong facility form, such as using the hospital form for Community Physicians records


-


Incomplete authorization for sensitive records, where mental health and substance use categories need explicit selection


-


Missing legal documentation when requesting on behalf of someone else, such as power of attorney, guardianship papers, or representative documentation


Incomplete or improperly completed forms can delay processing or require correction before the request can be fulfilled. Codes Health's AI validation identifies authorization and date-range issues before submission, which cuts down on avoidable provider rejections and resubmission delays.

## **Older and Childhood Records**


### **Pediatric and Teen Records**


-


Parents can access a minor child's records through MyChart proxy access


-


For teens ages 13 to 17, Johns Hopkins provides parents or guardians proxy access with limited visibility because of teen privacy protections


-


Adults requesting their own childhood records use the standard patient request form


-


Access can depend on parental rights and any applicable custody orders. Contact Hopkins HIM if custody documentation affects authority to request the record


### **Retention and Archived Records**


For Maryland records, state law generally requires medical records to be kept at least seven years after creation, with additional protections for minors' records, which generally cannot be destroyed until the patient turns 18 plus seven years, subject to statutory exceptions and notice requirements.


Older records may take longer depending on availability and storage format. Use broad date ranges when exact treatment dates are unknown, note on the form that you are seeking historical records, and call the HIM office directly if the treatment predates electronic systems.


Codes Health uses provider and facility data to identify where records exist, which matters most on cases with multiple treating facilities or a client whose recollection of their care history is incomplete.


## **Verifying Completeness After Records Arrive**


### **Identifying Gaps**


Check that all requested date ranges are covered, every facility where care occurred is represented, the specific record types you asked for are present, and billing documentation lines up with the clinical timeline. Initial requests often come back incomplete when a client was treated at multiple Hopkins facilities and each needed its own request.


### **Requesting the Missing Pieces**


Identify exactly what is absent, contact the HIM office to confirm whether additional records exist, submit a supplemental request, and reference the original request number if you have one.


Codes Health reviews retrieved batches for completeness against the original request and flags missing-record gaps for follow-up before closing out a retrieval.


## **Mental Health, Substance Use, and Billing Requests**


### **Mental Health Records**


Psychiatric and psychological records use the mental health authorization, Form A.2.1.l, which contains selections for behavioral health records, psychiatric admission notes, psychiatric evaluations and diagnoses, psychological and educational reports, progress notes, and drug and alcohol treatment records.


Psychotherapy notes are a separate matter. Under HIPAA they receive special protection and are excluded from the ordinary individual right of access, and most uses or disclosures of separately maintained psychotherapy notes require specific authorization, subject to limited exceptions.


Johns Hopkins states that if a patient is under psychiatric care, the request must be reviewed by the psychiatrist or designee before release. If release is denied, a summary from the psychiatrist may be obtained by written request to HIM.


Certain substance use disorder records maintained by federally assisted programs receive additional protections under[42 CFR Part 2](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-2) . Updated Part 2 requirements became mandatory on February 16, 2026. Part 2 protects records held by those programs rather than every chart that mentions substance use.


### **Billing Records**


Attorney requests for hospital billing records follow a separate path. Johns Hopkins processes them through Patient Financial Services via Datavant, with its own submission instructions, and says to allow 30 days. Clinical authorization forms also contain billing-record selections, but do not assume checking that box routes an attorney billing request correctly.


Codes Health supports medical, billing, and imaging requests through one workflow, which consolidates the documentation needed for case valuation, demand preparation, and litigation.


## **Notes for Legal Practitioners**


Hopkins record requests from a firm need a patient-signed authorization specific to third-party release, and language covering the full designated record set including nursing notes, MAR, amendments, and addenda. If certification matters for your case, ask the applicable HIM department whether it is available and whether extra charges apply.


On priority handling, Johns Hopkins states that requests related to direct patient care, such as records needed for a scheduled medical appointment, receive priority. It does not state that litigation deadlines or attorney cover letters qualify.


For deceased patients, representatives must provide documentation establishing their authority. Hopkins forms recognize a court-appointed personal representative, executor, or administrator. Confirm with the applicable HIM office whether additional documentation such as a death certificate is required for that request.


Multi-facility coordination is where firms lose the most time. A client who had emergency care at one Hopkins location, surgery at another, and rehabilitation at a third needs three correctly addressed requests.


### **Provider Transfers and Health Information Exchanges**


Records sent directly to another physician or health care facility for continuing care are copied[at no charge](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/patient-care/patients-visitors/medical-records) .


Effective October 17, 2024, Johns Hopkins states that its facilities no longer share abortion-care information with other organizations through health information exchanges, consistent with Maryland SB 786. Patients can still see reproductive-care information in MyChart and share their records through the Sharing Hub.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **How long does it take to receive records from Johns Hopkins?**


Johns Hopkins says applicable law generally allows between 21 and 30 days depending on the state, and that requests often finish sooner. Under HIPAA, a covered entity generally must act on an individual access request within 30 calendar days, with one possible 30-day extension after written notice. Maryland law separately addresses disclosure within a reasonable time, with a 21-working-day provision tied to knowing refusal. Hopkins gives priority to requests related to direct patient care, such as records needed for a scheduled appointment.


### **Is there a fee for requesting records from Johns Hopkins?**


Johns Hopkins says a $6.50 fee may apply to electronically maintained records, and that paper or microfilm portions may be charged up to $0.12 per page plus a $0.90 flat labor fee. Third parties may also be charged a retrieval fee. Costs can vary by facility and are subject to change. Records sent to another provider for continuing care are copied at no charge, and MyChart access carries no fee. If you need certification, ask the applicable HIM department whether it is available and what it costs.


### **Can I request records for a family member?**


Yes, with proper authority. Parents can use MyChart proxy access or a formal authorization for a minor child. For incapacitated adults, provide proof of medical power of attorney or court-appointed guardianship. For a deceased patient, a court-appointed personal representative, executor, or administrator must provide documentation establishing authority, and you should confirm with HIM whether anything further, such as a death certificate, is needed. Where custody affects who may request the record, contact Hopkins HIM.


### **What if I find an error in my records?**


Submit the Request to Amend PHI form, Form A.6.3.a, describing the error and the correction you want. Johns Hopkins states it will respond within 60 days, with one possible extension of up to 30 days if it sends written notice explaining the delay. If the amendment is denied, you have the right to submit a statement of disagreement that becomes part of the record. In litigation, consider requesting relevant amendments, addenda, and corrected versions where available.


### **Can Johns Hopkins send records electronically?**


Yes. Select email as the delivery method on the authorization. Hopkins forms offer both encrypted and unencrypted email options, and patients choosing unencrypted email are warned of the security risks, so pick deliberately rather than assuming transmission is secured. Once records are downloaded to a personal device, the patient assumes responsibility for their security. Fax remains available for provider-to-provider transfers.


### **What form is required for mental health records?**


Psychiatric and psychological records use the mental health authorization, Form A.2.1.l, rather than the standard hospital release. Its selections cover behavioral health records, psychiatric admission notes, evaluations and diagnoses, psychological and educational reports, progress notes, and drug and alcohol treatment records. Psychotherapy notes are treated separately under HIPAA and are excluded from the ordinary right of access. If the patient is under psychiatric care, the request goes to the psychiatrist or designee for review before release, and a summary may be offered if release is denied.
